newsitem.title: USA: Bad weather keeps U.S. Air Force from crashed plane.
newsitem.headline: Bad weather keeps U.S. Air Force from crashed plane.

text.p: Foul weather on Monday prevented a search and rescue team from approaching the site where Air Force officials believe a missing A-10 Thunderbolt attack bomber crashed into a mountain more than two weeks ago.
"There are high winds, rain and snow in the higher elevations that prevent any kind of attempt to reach the wreckage right now," Air Force spokesman Lt. Keith Shepherd said.

The wreckage of a plane that officials said was "likely" the missing aircraft was spotted on Sunday by an Army National Guard helicopter crew near a steep cliff on New York Mountain in the remote Sawatch Range southeast of the Vail ski resort.

Shepherd said the weather forecast for the area "severely diminishes the chances of any sort of operation being mounted this week." He said the forecast for the rest of the week called for rain, snow and fog.

Conditions were so bad, he added, that an MH-53 heavy lift helicopter from Albuquerque, New Mexico, on its way to Eagle, Colorado, where the search headquarters are located, had to be diverted to Leadville, Colorado.

"I'm looking out of the window right now and there's heavy cloud cover over the mountains. I can't even see halfway up the mountains. We are not sending anybody up there in these conditions. We are not going to put anybody in harm's way," he said by telephone from Eagle.
He said once the weather cleared a team of search and rescue experts would be lowered from the MH-53 to the crash site so they could inspect the wreckage and determine whether it was the missing jet.
Maj. Gen. Nels Running said on Sunday the gray pieces with yellowish-green anti-corrosion undercoat appeared to be from the plane's interior. "It looks to us military," he said.

The discovery was made by Army National Guard Chief Warrant Officers Richard Rugg and Dale Jensen as they hovered 30 feet (10 metres) over a sheer cliff face. "The first thing we saw was just a couple of pieces of paper. Then something just caught my eye," Rugg said at the news briefing.
Maj. Chuck Mitchell, an A-10 pilot who flew over the site later in a helicopter to try to identify the wreckage, said he saw 18 to 24 pieces of metal, which looked like "pieces of a jigsaw puzzle."

The A-10 Thunderbolt with four 500-pound (225-kg) Mark 82 conventional bombs disappeared during a routine training mission on April 2. Air Force officials have been at a loss to explain why the pilot, Capt. Craig Button, 32, left the three-plane formation and apparently veered northeast into Colorado, some 850 miles (1,350 km) away.
